title: How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out
summary: A class in memory is only its data members, laid out by the alignment rules. Member functions, `static` members and access specifiers take no space in the object. Inheritance puts the base class's members first, and a class with virtual functions gains a hidden pointer at the front. Knowing this lets you read any object's bytes in a debugger.
ideas:
- Add a `virtual void update() {}` to `Entity` and run the offsets example again. Every offset shifts by 8, and `id` is no longer at 0.
- Reorder `Monster`'s members so that `level` comes before `health`. Does the size change? Why?
- In Visual Studio, create a `Monster` with known values and decode its bytes in the Memory window as in the table above.

cards.q: Which parts of a class take up space in each object?
cards.a:
Non-static data members, padding, and a vptr if it has virtuals

Member functions are code, stored once; static members live in static storage; access specifiers cost nothing.

cards.q: Why can a `Monster*` be used as an `Entity*` without changing the address?
cards.a:
With single inheritance the `Entity` subobject is at offset 0 of the `Monster`

The base comes first in the derived object's layout, so both pointers hold the same address.

A hidden argument holding the address of the object called on

On x64 Windows it arrives in the first argument register, `rcx`. It is a pointer, not a copy.

cards.q: A class has three `int` members, ten member functions and a `static int`. What is its `sizeof`?
cards.a:
12

Only the non-static data members are stored in each object.

cards.q: Where does a derived class's base subobject go?
cards.a:
At the start of the derived object, at offset 0

The base's members come first, so a pointer to the derived object is also a valid pointer to its base.

cards.q: Why is `sizeof(WithVirtual)` 16 when its only data member is an `int`?
cards.a:
A hidden 8-byte vptr is added, and the size is padded to 16

The vptr points to the class's table of virtual functions. The functions themselves are in the code section.

cards.q: How does a member function know which object it is working on?
cards.a:
The object's address is passed as a hidden argument, `this`

`obj.f(x)` is compiled much like `f(&obj, x)`.
